title: Negative (mostly): the ringed nematic rods travel only 13-18 px between divisions across 14 runs of 10 settings; 3 tracks on 3 seeds at zeta=1.0 reach 3.07-3.34 labkit body lengths then divide (1.5-1.8 rod lengths), so swim-then-divide on one individual sits at the M gate's edge
summary: With the self-made ring of 20261026T0200-c34-rodsource, the missing piece for C:swim-divide is one rod that swims >= 3 body lengths and then divides. swimdivide.py (labkit's own tracker) measures, for every track that ends in a split with two surviving children, its net displacement over its life. Over 14 runs (table.md: activity zeta 0.8-1.4, chemostat rate kr, bath level phi_b, viscosity eta, friction xi, nematic stiffness L, and a ring-gated CH mobility gm) the best track per run moves 0.4-3.3 labkit body lengths (0.2-1.8 rod lengths); the instantaneous speed is the same for small and large rods (0.2-0.26 px/frame), so the limit is speed times cycle time, and every knob that lengthens the cycle also slows the rods or stops nucleation. Only zeta=1.0 gives tracks past 3 labkit body lengths: 2 on seed 0, 0 on seed 1, 1 on seed 2 (strip_*.png: a ringed rod swims about 17 px and splits into two ringed daughters), and the ring still passes in 94-96% of body-frames there. Letting the ring throttle the rod's CH mobility (gm=5) does change the individual (speed 0.08 -> 0.03, persistent splits 19 -> 12, a ring that does work), but kills swimming.

finding.operator: extensile active stress on CH rods with a self-made surfactant ring; parameter scan of the swim-then-divide distance
finding.control: 10 settings x seed 0, zeta 0.8 and 1.0 on seeds 0-2; labkit tracker
finding.result: best net displacement between birth and division 0.37-3.34 labkit BL (0.22-1.78 rod lengths); tracks >= 3 labkit BL then dividing: 3 of 57 dividing tracks at zeta=1.0 over 3 seeds, 0 elsewhere
